questions.question: A laboratory isolate is a gram-negative bacillus. On triple sugar iron (TSI) agar it shows an alkaline slant with scant H2S production. It is citrate negative, lysine positive, and urease negative.
questions.question_raw: Isolate in the lab that is a GNB. On TSI, there is an alkaline slant with scant production of H2S. It is citrate negative, lysine positive and urease negative.

parts.text: Name three antigens you would test and briefly describe each.

parts_raw.text: 3 antigens that you would test and briefly describe each.

questions.model_answer: This biochemical profile (non-lactose fermenter, alkaline/acid or alkaline slant, urease negative, non-motile) fits Salmonella/Shigella-type enterics; serotyping with the following antigens confirms and classifies the isolate: (1) O (somatic) antigen – heat-stable lipopolysaccharide of the outer membrane; O group/serogroup determines species/serogroup (e.g., Salmonella O groups; Shigella serogroups A-D correspond to species). (2) H (flagellar) antigen – heat-labile protein of flagella; present in motile organisms such as Salmonella (may be diphasic, phases 1 and 2) and used for serotype assignment; absent in non-motile Shigella. (3) Vi (capsular) antigen – heat-labile polysaccharide capsule that masks the O antigen; characteristically present in Salmonella Typhi (and some Paratyphi C and Dublin) and is the basis of the typhoid Vi polysaccharide vaccine.
questions.beyond_mandell: O/H/Vi serotyping conventions per CDC/reference enteric bacteriology (Kauffmann–White scheme).

questions.question: Shigella diarrhea.

parts.text: List three immune-mediated complications following infection.

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Reactive arthritis (post-infectious/ReA, HLA-B27 associated; may include the Reiter triad of arthritis, conjunctivitis, urethritis). (2) Hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS)/thrombotic microangiopathy, associated with Shiga toxin–producing Shigella dysenteriae type 1. (3) Erythema nodosum (or Guillain-Barré syndrome as an alternative immune-mediated sequela).
b) (1) A fluoroquinolone – ciprofloxacin. (2) Azithromycin (ceftriaxone is an acceptable alternative, particularly where fluoroquinolone/multidrug resistance is prevalent). Choice should be guided by local resistance patterns and susceptibility testing.
questions.beyond_mandell: Complication list and antibiotic selection per Mandell and IDSA infectious diarrhea guidance.

cohort_answer.text:
Complications: HUS, reactive arthritis, febrile seizures, TTP
Treatment options: Azithromycin, cipro, ceftriaxone, amp, septra

questions.question: Shigella diarrhea.

parts.text: What are three immune-mediated complications of infection?
What are two treatment options, and when should they be considered?

parts_raw.text: a) What are 3 immune mediated complications of infection?
b) What are 2 treatment options? When should they be considered?

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Reactive arthritis (HLA-B27–associated post-infectious arthritis, ~2% of cases, may present as the Reiter triad). (2) Hemolytic uremic syndrome/thrombotic microangiopathy (Shiga toxin–mediated, chiefly S. dysenteriae type 1). (3) Ekiri syndrome (lethal toxic encephalopathy, seen mainly in children) – erythema nodosum or Guillain-Barré are acceptable alternatives.
b) (1) A fluoroquinolone (ciprofloxacin) or (2) azithromycin, with ceftriaxone as an alternative in regions of high resistance (e.g., parts of Asia); selection guided by in vitro susceptibility. When to consider: antimicrobial therapy is recommended for essentially all confirmed Shigella infections to shorten illness and reduce transmission, and is especially indicated in severe disease, dysentery, and immunocompromised or high-risk hosts. Typical duration: 3 days for a fluoroquinolone or azithromycin; ~5 days for ceftriaxone or SXT (longer, 7–10 days, in immunocompromised patients).
questions.beyond_mandell: Treatment thresholds and durations per IDSA infectious diarrhea guidance (2017).

cohort_answer.text:
HUS; Reactive arthritis; Encephalopathy (Ekiri syndrome - more in pediatrics, after S. sonnei or S. flexneri)
Macrolides or Fluoroquinolones (or ceftriaxone if from area with high resistance like Asia), based on in vitro susceptibility. All infections should be treated. Macrolide or FQ: 3 days; SXT or CTRX: 5 days

questions.question: According to CLSI 2016, which three antibiotics should be routinely tested and reported for Salmonella and Shigella isolated from stool (report for fecal typhoidal Salmonella [Typhi and Paratyphi] and Shigella)?
questions.question_raw: According to CLSI 2016, which 3 antibiotics should be tested and reported for Salmonella and Shigella isolated from stool? Report only for fecal typhoidal salmonella (typhi and paratyphi), and shigella.
questions.model_answer: (1) Ampicillin. (2) A fluoroquinolone (ciprofloxacin). (3) Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. For extraintestinal Salmonella isolates, a third-generation cephalosporin (and chloramphenicol) should additionally be reported.
questions.beyond_mandell: Based on CLSI M100 (2016) reporting guidance, not the chapter text.

cohort_answer.text: Ampicillin, Fluoroquinolones, Septra (if extraintestinal, also report 3rd gen cephalosporins; azithro has breakpoints now but not reported)

questions.question: Your organization uses MALDI-TOF for identification of bacteria. A girl presents with bloody diarrhea and the laboratory reports Shigella flexneri.
questions.question_raw: PM 7. Your organization uses MALDI-TOF for identification of bacteria. Girl presents with bloody diarrhea and reports Shigella flexneri

parts.text: Why should MALDI-TOF not be used for identification of this organism?
Explain the concept of mass spectrometry and how it allows identification.
Give three advantages and three disadvantages of MALDI-TOF.

parts_raw.text: Why should MALDI-TOF NOT be used for identification of this organism? (1)
Explain the concept of "mass spec" and how it allows identification. (2)

questions.model_answer:
a) Shigella is genetically a biochemically inactive Escherichia coli - the two share essentially identical ribosomal protein spectra, so MALDI-TOF cannot reliably distinguish Shigella species from E. coli; identification requires biochemicals and serotyping/molecular testing.
b) A colony is spotted on a target plate with an energy-absorbing matrix; a laser pulse desorbs and ionizes predominantly abundant ribosomal proteins. The charged proteins are accelerated through a vacuum flight tube in an electric field, and time of flight to the detector varies with mass-to-charge ratio (larger ions fly more slowly). The resulting mass spectrum is a species-specific fingerprint matched against a reference database, generating an identification with a confidence score.
c) Advantages: (1) Very rapid - identification in minutes from a colony, shortening time to optimal therapy. (2) Very low consumable cost per test and less technologist hands-on time than biochemical panels. (3) Accurate and objective across a broad range of bacteria, yeasts, mycobacteria and moulds, including fastidious and anaerobic organisms poorly identified by biochemicals. Disadvantages: (1) High capital cost and need for expertise/maintenance. (2) Identification limited to organisms in the reference database, which is incomplete for some moulds, anaerobes and rare species. (3) Cannot discriminate closely related organisms (Shigella vs E. coli, Streptococcus pneumoniae vs mitis/oralis) and provides no susceptibility data.

cohort_answer.text: Shigella too similar to E. coli (metabolically-challenged E. coli, same ribosomal proteins) - MALDI not reliable. Mass spec: colony placed on matrix, laser causes desorption/ionization of rRNA macroprotein; fragments ionized and accelerated in electromagnetic field, hit detector based on mass:charge ratio (bigger proteins = slower flight, time of flight TOF); spectra unique fingerprint compared to standardized database. Advantages: rapid identification, limited need for lab personnel, highly accurate, less subjective than biochemicals. Disadvantages: organism needs to be in database, does not give susceptibility patterns, expensive machine, unable to identify very closely related organisms (e.g. Strep mitis/oralis, E. coli/Shigella).

questions.question: Shigella dysenteriae.

parts.text: What are two empiric treatment options?

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Hemolytic uremic syndrome/thrombotic microangiopathy (Shiga toxin–mediated, characteristic of S. dysenteriae type 1). (2) Reactive arthritis (HLA-B27 associated, post-infectious). (3) Erythema nodosum (or Guillain-Barré syndrome as an alternative immune-mediated sequela).
b) (1) Ciprofloxacin (fluoroquinolone – empiric treatment of choice). (2) Ceftriaxone or azithromycin as alternatives, particularly where fluoroquinolone resistance is common; de-escalate per susceptibility.
questions.beyond_mandell: Empiric agents per Mandell and IDSA infectious diarrhea guidance.

questions.question: Match each stool pathogen to its microbiological features. Features: (i) microaerophilic, grows on charcoal; (ii) H2S-producing non-lactose fermenter, catalase-negative (possibly oxidase-negative) curved gram-negative bacillus; (iii) non-lactose fermenter, catalase-negative (possibly oxidase-negative). Organisms: Vibrio, Shigella sonnei, Salmonella typhimurium, Campylobacter, Aeromonas.
questions.question_raw:
Q41 (2013 AM)
Stool pathogens, various microbiological features, match pathogen to features. Micro features given: Microaerophilic grows on charcoal; H2S producing NLF, catalase negative (maybe oxidase negative) curved GNB; NLF catalase negative (may be oxidase negative). Organisms: Vibrio, Shigella sonnei, Salmonella typhimurium, Campylobacter, Aeromonas

parts.text: Match each pathogen to its microbiological features.

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Microaerophilic, grows on charcoal = Campylobacter (spiral/vibrioid gram-negative rod, thermophilic 42 C, oxidase and catalase positive, requires microaerobic incubation and selective/charcoal media). (2) H2S-producing non-lactose fermenter = Salmonella typhimurium (facultatively anaerobic Enterobacteriaceae, oxidase-negative, produces H2S). (3) Non-lactose fermenter, catalase-negative/oxidase-negative = Shigella sonnei (nonmotile, no H2S). Vibrio and Aeromonas are oxidase-positive non-lactose fermenters and do not fit these three cues.
questions.beyond_mandell: Only the Campylobacter microbiology (microaerophilic, charcoal/selective media, oxidase/catalase-positive vibrioid morphology) is from this chapter; the Salmonella, Shigella, Vibrio and Aeromonas features rest on standard clinical microbiology (Manual of Clinical Microbiology).

cohort_answer.text: Microaerophilic grows on charcoal - Campylobacter. H2S producing NLF, catalase negative (maybe oxidase negative) curved GNB - Salmonella. NLF catalase negative (may be oxidase negative) - Shigella. Additional detail: Vibrio - gram negative, non-lactose fermenter, curved-rod (comma) shape, facultative anaerobe, oxidase positive, motile with polar flagella. Shigella sonnei - nonmotile, facultatively anaerobic GNR, non-lactose fermenter, no H2S, indole positive, ferments glucose/urea, oxidase negative, differentiated by ornithine decarboxylase expression. Salmonella typhimurium - gram negative facultatively anaerobic Enterobacteriaceae, non-lactose fermenter, oxidase negative, produces H2S. Campylobacter - spiral shape, long flagella, mostly microaerophilic, thermophilic, nonfermentative, oxidase and catalase positive, urease negative (vs Helicobacter urease positive). Aeromonas - gram negative, non-lactose fermenter, oxidase positive, ferments glucose

questions.question: Shigella dysenteriae.
questions.model_answer: a) (1) Reactive arthritis (HLA-B27–associated post-infectious arthritis, may include conjunctivitis and urethritis – Reiter triad). (2) Hemolytic uremic syndrome/thrombotic microangiopathy (Shiga toxin–producing S. dysenteriae type 1). (3) Erythema nodosum (Guillain-Barré syndrome and Ekiri toxic encephalopathy are additional recognized immune-mediated sequelae).

cohort_answer.text: Reactive arthritis, conjunctivitis, urethritis (post-infectious arthritis in ~2% of S. flexneri infections, requires genetic predisposition); Ekiri syndrome (lethal toxic encephalopathy); Erythema nodosum; GN; Guillain Barre syndrome; HUS/TTP (associated with Shiga toxin-producing Shigella, most often S. dysenteriae) (speaker notes: Ekiri syndrome, erythema nodosum, GBS)

questions.question: Shigella dysenteriae.

parts.text: What are two empiric treatment options?

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Ciprofloxacin (fluoroquinolone – treatment of choice empirically). (2) Ceftriaxone or azithromycin (if susceptible) as alternatives, favored where fluoroquinolone/multidrug resistance is prevalent. Duration: ~3 days for a fluoroquinolone or azithromycin, ~5 days for a beta-lactam such as ceftriaxone; 7–10 days in immunocompromised patients. Narrow therapy per susceptibility results.
questions.beyond_mandell: Durations per IDSA infectious diarrhea guidance.

cohort_answer.text: Ceftriaxone; FQ (Cipro is treatment of choice); Azithromycin (if susceptible). Duration: 5 days for beta lactam, 3 days for azithro/FQ; immunocompromised treat 7-10 days

questions.question: Match each microbiological description to the correct stool pathogen. Pathogen options: Vibrio cholerae, Shigella sonnei, Salmonella typhimurium, Campylobacter, Aeromonas.
questions.question_raw: Stool pathogens, various microbiological features, match pathogen to features. Micro descriptions (4) and pathogens (5 – Vibrio, Shigella sonnei, Salmonella typhimurium, Campylobacter, Aeromonas)

parts.text: Micro 1 - microaerophilic, grows on charcoal-based selective media.
Micro 3 - non-lactose fermenter, catalase-negative, curved gram-negative bacillus.
Micro 4 - non-lactose fermenter, catalase-negative, biochemically inert.

parts_raw.text: Micro 1 - microaerophilic, grows on charcoal something something
Micro 3 - NLF, catalase negative curved GNB

questions.model_answer: a) Campylobacter (e.g. C. jejuni) - microaerophilic, grows on charcoal- or blood-based selective media (Skirrow/CCDA) at 42 degrees C. b) Salmonella typhimurium - H2S producing (black colonies on XLD/Hektoen/SS agar), non-lactose fermenter. c) Vibrio cholerae - non-lactose fermenter, comma/curved gram-negative rod, oxidase-positive facultative anaerobe growing on TCBS/alkaline peptone water. d) Shigella sonnei - non-lactose (or late-lactose) fermenting, non-motile, biochemically inert enteric. Aeromonas is the unused distractor.
questions.beyond_mandell: Only the Vibrio descriptors (curved GNR, oxidase-positive, selective media) are in this chapter; the Campylobacter, Salmonella, and Shigella identifications rest on standard clinical microbiology (Mandell species chapters / Manual of Clinical Microbiology).

cohort_answer.text:
Campylobacter
Salmonella typhimurium
Vibrio
Shigella sonnei
